item.title: Antisymmetric contractions vanish and $mU'=q\Phi(U)$ preserves $\eta(U,U)$
item.statement:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature $(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V	imes V	o\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form, $F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$ ([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]], [[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and $\Phi:V	o V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with $F_{\alpha eta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_ eta)$ in a frame $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha eta}u^ eta$, the index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_
u u^
u=0$. Consequently, if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J	o V$ is differentiable ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on $J$ for some real $m
e0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$ defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field $F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any particle.
item.strategy: For each $u$, $w\mapsto F(w,u)$ is a linear functional. The nondegenerate finite-dimensional form $\eta$ identifies $V$ with $V^*$, so it gives a unique $\Phi(u)$; bilinearity and uniqueness make $\Phi$ linear. In a frame, evaluating the defining pairing at $w=e_\alpha$ gives $\eta_{\alpha\mu}\Phi(u)^\mu=F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, hence $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$. Taking $w=u$ gives $\eta(\Phi(u),u)=F(u,u)=0$ by skew-symmetry, and symmetry of $\eta$ gives $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$. For the norm claim $f(s):=\eta(U(s),U(s))=\sum_a\epsilon_a(U^a(s))^2$, with $\epsilon=(-1,1,1,1)$, satisfies $f'=2\eta(U,U')$ by the product rule. The equation gives $\eta(U,U')=(q/m)\eta(U,\Phi(U))=0$, so the zero-derivative theorem on the open interval $J$ makes $f$ constant. The identical pointwise calculation with $\Phi_s$ proves the varying-form clause: differentiate $\eta(U,U)$ only, not $F_s$ or $\Phi_s$. No constant-field assumption is used in that clause.

item.title: Explicit mathematical hypothesis/convention examples
item.statement: With $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: (i) $v=(1,0,0,0)$ is future timelike and unit, $\eta(v,v)=-1$. (ii) For $0<\beta<1$ the boost $\Lambda_\beta$ of [[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]] sends $v$ to $(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$, whose $\eta$-norm is $-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$ and whose time component $\gamma$ is positive; at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined, so the hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ cannot be dropped. (iii) The null line $z(s)=(s,s,0,0)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, has $\eta(z',z')=0$, so the proper-time construction of [[lem-em-proper-time-reparametrization]] gives $\tau\equiv0$, which is not an invertible parameter: the timelike hypothesis cannot be weakened to causal. (iv) For the symmetric nonzero form $F:=\eta$ one has $\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ and $\eta(v,\Phi(v))=\eta(v,v)=-1\ne0$, so the antisymmetry hypothesis of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] is genuine. (v) For the skew form with $F_{01}=1$, $F_{10}=-1$ and other coefficients zero, the operator of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] sends $e_0$ to $-e_1$: $\eta(-e_1,w)=-w^1=F(w,e_0)$. Thus its invariant pairing and standard raised-index formula have the same sign, and $\eta(e_0,\Phi(e_0))=0$. No physical clock premise or experimental claim is used.
item.strategy: Five direct computations in the fixed standard frame: evaluation of $\eta$ on the given vectors, substitution of $v$ in the boost formula, the vanishing of the null tangent, and the identification $\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ when $F=\eta$ (uniqueness in the defining property of $\Phi$). For (v), the first column of $\eta^{-1}F$ is $(0,-1,0,0)$; both pairings equal $-w^1$, and the time-space orthogonality is immediate. All are exact finite computations; no source or physical assumption is needed.

item.title: Elapsed proper time is invariant under increasing C^1 reparametrizations
item.statement: Let c > 0, let x: I -> A be a C^1 future timelike worldline, let a < b with [a,b] contained in I, and let c_0 < d_0. Let phi: [c_0,d_0] -> [a,b] be a strictly increasing C^1 surjection, with one-sided endpoint derivatives as in def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline. Then phi(c_0)=a, phi(d_0)=b and phi' >= 0. Put y=x o phi and f(s)=sqrt(-eta(x'(s),x'(s))). The C^1 curve y has tangent y'(u)=phi'(u)x'(phi(u)), future timelike exactly where phi'(u)>0 and zero where phi'(u)=0. Its nonnegative length integrand is sqrt(-eta(y'(u),y'(u)))=phi'(u)f(phi(u)); this integrand is defined even when y is not a worldline. The broad substitution identity is integral_{c_0}^{d_0} sqrt(-eta(y',y')) du = integral_a^b f(s) ds = c(tau_x(b)-tau_x(a)). If phi'(u)>0 at every point, including the one-sided endpoints, y is a C^1 future timelike worldline, its proper-time function tau_y is defined by def-sr-proper-time, and tau_y(d_0)-tau_y(c_0)=tau_x(b)-tau_x(a). More generally tau_y(u)-tau_y(v)=tau_x(phi(u))-tau_x(phi(v)) for all v,u in [c_0,d_0], so tau_y and tau_x o phi differ by a base-point constant. No tau_y is asserted for a zero-tangent curve outside that definition. For a strictly decreasing C^1 surjection phi onto [a,b], phi(c_0)=b, phi(d_0)=a and phi'<=0. The tangent of y is past timelike where phi'<0 and zero where phi'=0, so y is not a future timelike worldline. Its nonnegative length integral still equals integral_a^b f(s) ds: oriented substitution gives integral_{c_0}^{d_0} phi' f(phi)=integral_b^a f, and |phi'|=-phi' reverses that sign. These are mathematical curve-integral identities; physical clock reading is a separate premise.
item.strategy: By the componentwise chain rule, including its one-sided endpoint reading, y'=phi'(x' o phi). Bilinearity gives -eta(y',y')=(phi')^2(-eta(x' o phi,x' o phi)), so the nonnegative square root is |phi'|(f o phi). The function f is continuous on I by def-sr-proper-time, and the C^1 derivative phi' is continuous and therefore Riemann integrable on its compact interval. The published thm-substitution applies with f and phi even when phi' vanishes: for increasing phi its oriented endpoints are a,b and |phi'|=phi', proving the broad integral equality. The future cone is preserved by a positive scalar; at phi'=0 the tangent is zero, which is excluded by the worldline definition. Thus only the everywhere-positive derivative case permits applying def-sr-proper-time to y. Apply substitution on every subinterval [v,u] (with oriented reversal when u<v) to prove the proper-time difference formula and base-point constant. For decreasing phi, oriented endpoints b,a give the negative integral, while |phi'|=-phi' restores the positive integral; the tangent is past timelike where the scalar is negative and zero otherwise. No inverse of phi and no nonvanishing derivative are needed for the broad integral identities. No choice principle is used.

item.title: Worked example: invariance of elapsed proper time under a cubic reparametrization
item.statement: Worked computation. In an inertial chart with eta_0 = diag(-1,1,1,1) let d := (5,3,0,0), a future timelike displacement with -eta(d,d) = 25 - 9 = 16 and sqrt(-eta(d,d)) = 4. (a) The worldline x(s) := s d on the parameter interval [1,8] has x'(s) = d, integrand sqrt(-eta(d,d)) = 4, and elapsed proper time tau(8) - tau(1) = (1/c) integral_1^8 4 ds = 28/c. (b) The reparametrization phi(u) := u^3 is a strictly increasing C^1 surjection of [1,2] onto [1,8]; its derivative 3u^2 is strictly positive throughout [1,2], so the reparametrized curve y(u) := x(u^3) = u^3 d has y'(u) = 3u^2 d, hence sqrt(-eta(y',y')) = 3u^2 sqrt(-eta(d,d)) = 12u^2, and elapsed proper time (1/c) integral_1^2 12u^2 du = (4/c)(8 - 1) = 28/c. The two elapsed times agree, as lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance requires, and the proper-time function of x is tau(s) = 4s/c up to an additive constant, with inverse rho(tau) = c(tau - tau_0)/4, where tau_0 is the chosen additive constant. (c) Boundary check: instead take the same straight curve x(s)=s d on [-1,1] and phi(u)=u^3 on [-1,1]. This is a strictly increasing C^1 surjection, but y'(0)=0, so y is not a worldline of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline. The broad length-integral identity nevertheless holds: integral_{-1}^{1} 12u^2 du=8=integral_{-1}^{1} 4 ds. No proper-time function of y is invoked outside its defining worldline domain.
item.strategy: Two independent exact computations of the same elapsed time: in (a) the integrand is the constant 4; in (b) the chain rule gives y' = 3u^2 d and the integrand 12u^2, whose integral over [1,2] is 28. The equality is the concrete instance of the invariance lemma, and the inverse function is read off the linear proper-time function. All arithmetic is rational. On [1,2], 3u^2>=3>0 verifies the strengthened worldline consequence. For the boundary interval [-1,1], differentiate u^3 d to obtain the zero tangent at zero, and integrate 12u^2 to get 8; this checks precisely the distinction between the broad substitution identity and the regular-worldline consequence.

item.title: Worked example: four-velocity and four-acceleration of uniform circular motion
item.statement: Worked computation. In an inertial chart with eta_0 = diag(-1,1,1,1) let R > 0 and omega be real with R|omega| < c and consider the worldline x(t) = (c t, R cos(omega t), R sin(omega t), 0), parametrized by coordinate time: uniform circular motion in the first two spatial coordinates. Then w(t) = (-R omega sin(omega t), R omega cos(omega t), 0) has |w| = R|omega|, so -eta(x',x') = c^2 - R^2 omega^2 and the proper-time factor is tau' = c^{-1} sqrt(c^2 - R^2 omega^2) = 1/gamma with gamma := (1 - R^2 omega^2/c^2)^{-1/2}; the four-velocity is U = gamma (c, w). Since |w| is constant, gamma is constant; the coordinate acceleration is a(t) = (-R omega^2 cos(omega t), -R omega^2 sin(omega t), 0), with |a| = R omega^2 and w.a = 0. By clause (e) of thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition the four-acceleration is A = (0, gamma^2 a), so A^0 = 0, eta(U,A) = 0 and eta(A,A) = gamma^4 R^2 omega^4 >= 0. Its magnitude is gamma^2 R omega^2; for R>0 it is spacelike exactly when omega!=0, while omega=0 is the static limit with gamma=1, U=(c,0,0,0) and A=0. Numerical specialization: if R omega = 3c/5, then gamma = 5/4 and the magnitude of the four-acceleration is gamma^2 R omega^2 = (25/16) R omega^2 = (15 c omega)/16.
item.strategy: Finite computation: differentiate the coordinate path, evaluate the diagonal quadratic form to get tau', read gamma, and apply clause (e) of the theorem with w.a = 0 to obtain A = gamma^2 a; the numerical values are exact rational multiples of c and omega. The acceleration is centripetal and orthogonal to the velocity, so the four-acceleration is orthogonal to the four-velocity by the theorem. Since R>0 and gamma>0, gamma^4 R^2 omega^4 is zero exactly when omega=0 and positive otherwise. At zero frequency the path is (ct,R,0,0) and both the coordinate and four-acceleration vanish. The specialization R omega=3c/5 has omega>0 and preserves the displayed exact value and acceleration units.
